body:
# Skuld versus the internet

*Court is in session. In the matter of Skuld, the register hears the evidence — the attestation, the marks, and the forms that stand accused.*

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Skuld
- **Original script:** ᛋᚴᚢᛚᛏ
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Convention:** normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 340 of 406

## The Charge

That the name **Skuld** is routinely written in forms that move, drop, or invent its marks — and that each such form teaches the reader a different, lesser name. The register's task is to separate the honest fallback from the outright false.

## The Defense of the Canonical Form

The attested form is **ᛋᚴᚢᛚᛏ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Skuld**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them demands.

## The Character Witness

The plain form *skuld* differs from the canonical **Skuld** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## Mitigating Circumstances

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Skuld**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Old Norse orthography is a primary source in itself: þ (thorn) and ð (eth) are letters the language used natively, not transliteration marks — English once had them too, and lost them. ǫ (o with ogonek) is a nasal vowel with its own saga-era history, and normalized Old Norse spelling preserves it because the Eddas' editors do. To write th for þ or o for ǫ is not modernization; it is a different spelling of a different word. The Eddic poems survive in one manuscript tradition each — the register spells the names the way those manuscripts do.

## Registration, Honestly

Three facts govern every domain this project registers. One: IDNA 2008 welcomes the marks — punycode encodes them legally and browsers show them faithfully. Two: welcome is not availability — registrars hold partial inventory, so the ideal form of a name may exist in the protocol yet not in the shop window today. Three: typeability is a separate virtue — a form no one can type on a phone is a form no one will visit, however canonical.

Hence the hierarchy the rulebook enforces: take the most complete form that is *both* attested and *actually registrable*, and never accept a wrong mark for the sake of availability. The wrong accent is not a rung on that ladder; it is off the ladder entirely.

## The Verdict

So the register finds: **Skuld**, canonical; *skuld*, equally canonical; the contested forms, recorded with their support; the false forms, ruled against with their violations named. Every line of that finding cites its evidence, and the evidence is open to any reader — the register asks to be checked, not trusted. The temple keeps the canonical form at [/skuld/](/skuld/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Poetic Edda: Völuspá 19–20 (the ash, the well, and the three maidens — Urðr, Verðandi, Skuld — who lay laws and choose lives) and 30 (Skuld bearing a shield in the tally of valkyries), trans. Carolyne Larrington, Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 15–16 (Urðarbrunnr and the three norns; the white clay that preserves the tree) and 36 (Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, ride to choose the slain), trans. Anthony Faulkes; Skáldskaparmál þulur (norna heiti, valkyrja heiti), Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. skuld ('debt, duty; a Norn'); Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, s.v. skuld.
